newsitem.title: UK: IRA cessation opens up new politial vistas.
newsitem.headline: IRA cessation opens up new politial vistas.

text.p: A newly called Irish Republican Army (IRA) ceasefire, effective from midday on Sunday, will generate a burst of activity in flagging Anglo-Irish peace efforts in Northern Ireland.
Britain is expected to end a ban on ministerial contact with Sinn Fein which it imposed in February 1996 after the IRA abandoned an intial ceasefire that lasted 18 months.

The Northern Ireland Office, in a July 9 letter to Sinn Fein, held out the prospect of resumed face-to-face talks and meetings between Sinn Fein and George Mitchell, a former U.S.senator chairing difficult multi-party talks.

The NIO said that "ministers will meet Sinn Fein in the period immediately following a ceasefire and will also encourage the Independent Chairman (Mitchell) to hold early meetings with Sinn Fein in this period".

The letter, which London published on Wednesday, reiterated Britain's policy that the IRA must call an unequivocal end to violence before Sinn Fein would be given a place in the Mitchell talks, which were launched in June, 1996.
On Monday, David Trimble, leader of the main pro-British Ulster Unionist Party, is scheduled to have talks with British Prime Minister Tony Blair in London.
Trimble says that British and Irish plans to achieve IRA disarmament are too vague.

The UUP threatens to oppose the plans in a key vote at a session of the talks in Belfast next Wednesday which has to adopt proposals from Britain and Ireland which call for the guerrillas to disarm while the talks progress instead of before or at the end.

The talks group Trimble's UUP, the hardline Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) of Ian Paisley, the small United Kingdom Unionist Party (UKUP), the moderate Irish nationalist SDLP party of John Hume and the middle of the road Alliance Party.
Unionists are furious that Sinn Fein will take a place at the talks without surrendering a single gun but only the UUP and UKUP have threatened to walk out of the negotiations.
Also included are the Ulster Democratic Party and Progressive Unionist Party, the political spokesmen of the IRA's ideological foes, Loyalist extremist groups who want the province to stay British.
The other two parties are a womens' coalition and the small Labour party.
Under British and Irish plans, Sinn Fein must sign up to the "Mitchell Principles", a code of non-violence and democratic tenets that all other parties in the talks support.
Britain said in a statement on June 28 said that Sinn Fein could be invited to substantive all party talks six weeks after declaration of an unequivocal end to violence.

Britain wants the Mitchell talks to break new ground by moving into a new phase of all-party negotiations on September 15. The IRA ceasefire appears to open the way for Sinn Fein admission to those talks.

Britain says talks on a new political settlement for the province should be concluded by May, 1998, when it would be tested in a referendum. The plan envisages a regional assembly with limited powers and cross-border bodies on trade, tourism and other matters to build new trust between the two Irelands and to blur the border the IRA wants to tear down and Unionists want to keep.
